sections.heading: Design of a New Piezoelectric Energy Harvester Based on Secondary Impact
sections.text:
HYUN JUN JUNG, KI HWAN BAEK, SINICHI HIDAKA, DANIEL SONG, SE BIN KIM, AND TAE HYUN SUNG\*

Departments of Electric Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul 133-791, Korea

Two models for an energy harvester imparting rotational energy to piezoelectric materials are presented, in order to compare the effects of applying identical amounts of energy to a cantilever beam by changing the total displacement per unit time, and applying a secondary impact. For a piezoelectric energy harvester given a high total impulse per unit time with low total displacement per unit time, higher power outputs were generated at lower resistive loads. Conversely, for a harvester given high total displacement per unit time with low total impulse per unit time, power output was higher at high resistive loads. At matched impedance, the secondary-impact-type piezoelectric energy harvester generated higher power output than the hitting-type piezoelectric energy harvester did at low resistive load. Optimized response of secondary-impact-type piezoelectric energy harvester was obtained at a frequency of $6 0 H z$ with a low resistive load of 1 kΩ. The generated output power was measured as $I 2 4 m W ,$ which corresponds to power density of 140 mW/cm² for the entire cantilever beam, and a power density of 342 mW/cm² for only the piezoelectric material volume (including sliver paste volume). For a harvester without a secondary impulse at low resistive loads $( l \ k \Omega )$ , the optimizing frequency was between 20 and $3 0 \ : H z$ , with an output power of $2 2 m W ,$ which corresponds to a 25 mW/cm² power density for entire cantilever beam and power density of 60 mW/cm3 for only the piezoelectric material volume(including sliver paste volume).

Keywords energy harvesting; piezoelectric; secondary; impact

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Energy harvesting has been actively studied, using piezoelectric conversion from mechanical energy to electrical energy. [12]. Several studies in particular have assessed shock and impact type piezoelectric energy harvesters [36].

The objective of the study described here was to compare differences in the application of total displacement per unit time and total impulse per unit time to a cantilever beam in the condition where the external energy remains the same. In this paper, two optimized energy harvesting models imparting rotational energy to piezoelectric materials are presented. In the first model (the "hitting type piezoelectric energy harvester"), a cantilever beam made of a piezoelectric material is struck repeatedly using a motor-driven stick and then a cantilever beam was vibrating freely. The second model (the "secondary impact type piezoelectric energy harvester") involves applying a secondary, discrete impulse using a fixed stick to stop vibration in the beam at the point where it has returned to its initial position (i.e., at its position of maximum kinetic energy). By using a fixed stick, it is possible to deliver the discrete impulse to the cantilever beam while it was at stopped vibration.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental Procedure
sections.text: A $1 \mathrm { N m }$ torque DC-power motor with a maximum rotational speed of $1 1 0 0 \mathrm { r p m } \left( 1 8 . 3 3 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ was used to power the strikes on the cantilever beam. A Tektronix DPO-3014 Oscilloscope was used as a voltmeter, and an OMRON ZS Smart Sensor was used to measure displacement. The piezoelectric material in the cantilever beam was manufactured by Higlobe Corporation, Korea. All of measurements were taken over 10 second periods. The secondary impact type harvester was designed so that a discrete impulse would be applied to the cantilever beam when it returned to its starting position, rather than the cantilever beam was vibrating freely. Thus, the secondary impact type harvester was designed to apply a higher total impulse per unit time with lower total displacement per unit time than the hitting type harvester. To apply the discrete impact, a fixed stick was utilized as shown in Fig. 2. The power and displacement of vibrations within the piezoelectric material are measured both as the motor-driven strikes are delivered and then upon delivery of the secondary impact.

sections.heading: A. Comparison of Free Vibration and Secondary Impact in the Open-Circuit
sections.text:
The Cantilever beam was set to an impact depth of $2 \mathrm { m m }$ , and cantilever beam was struck by a motor-driven "hitting stick" with a frequency of $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ (Fig. 2). The $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ frequency was chosen to clearly measure the decay of free vibrational motion following a strike until vibration had stopped, making an analysis of the free vibrational cycle simpler. Power and displacement in the secondary impact type harvester were measured between the strikes and the discrete impulse caused by the fixed stick. The experiment was conducted in open-circuit conditions.

On top of the cantilever beam is the piezelectricmaterial; bottom of the cantileverbeamis made of stainless steel (sus-301), (b) schematic diagram of the secondary impact type harvester, and (c) schematic diagram of the hitting type harvester (Color figure available online).

sections.heading: C. Optimization
sections.text: On the basis of the above results, it was found that for a striking cycle of $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { s }$ , the time duration of conversion of mechanical energy to electrical energy was $0 . 0 1 5 { - } 0 . 0 2 ~ \mathrm { s }$ in the secondary impact type harvester, and $0 . 2 \mathrm { - } 0 . 3 \ \mathrm { s }$ in the hitting type harvester. These results show electrical energy being generated over $3- 4 \%$ of the striking cycle in the secondary impact type harvester and over $4 0 { - } 6 0 \%$ of the striking cycle in the hitting type harvester. For each of these harvesters, it is expected that an optimizing output condition can be obtained when the striking cycle equals the duration of piezoelectric electricity generation. Additional experiments were conducted to measure the power output and displacement of both harvesters under striking frequencies from $2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ to $7 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and with resistive loads of $1 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $1 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and 1 MΩ. Resonance frequency matching was not taken into consideration in any of the experiments described here [8].

The maximum power output of the secondary impact type harvester was $4 . 7 5 \mathrm { m W } ,$ occurring at $3 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ ; this was higher than the maximum power of $4 . 0 9 \mathrm { m W }$ generated by the hitting type harvester at $1 0 \mathbf { k } \Omega$ Fig. 5 shows the output power generated by the two harvesters at a frequency of $2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and a resistive load of $3 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . From Figs. 5(b), (d), and (f), it can be seen that secondary impact type harvester generated most of the power output within 0.02 s of the striking time (0.110.13 s), during which the displacement on the cantilever beam went from a maximum value of $1 1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ to $0 \mathrm { m m }$ . For the hitting type harvester, Figs. 5(a), (c), and (e) show that most power generation occurred between $0 . 2 \mathrm { - } 0 . 3 \ \mathrm { s }$ (with output peaks from $0 . 0 0 { - } 0 . 0 5 ~ \mathrm { s }$ and from 0.10.2 s). For a secondary impact type harvester given a high total impulse per unit time with low total displacement per unit time, power output was higher than with the hitting type harvester at lower resistive loads. Conversely, for the hitting type harvester with high total displacement per unit time at a low total impulse per unit time, power output was higher than secondary impact type harvester at high resistive loads. At matched impedance, the secondary impact type harvester generated a higher power output than the hitting type harvester did at low resistive load.

sections.heading: C. Optimization
sections.text:
Figure 6 shows the power outputs of both the secondary impact type harvester and the hitting type harvester, measured from $2 \mathrm { H z }$ to $7 0 \mathrm { H z }$ at resistive loads of $1 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , $1 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ Fig. 6(a) shows the power output of the secondary impact type harvester linearly increasing as the striking frequency increases. In this case, an optimizing frequency was $6 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and output power was $1 2 4 { \mathrm { ~ m W } } ,$ which was in line with a predicted optimal range of $5 0 – 6 6 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ Figs. 7(a) and 7(b) show peak output power was $3 . 2 ~ \mathrm { W }$ at $6 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ with a $1 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistive load. For the hitting type harvester, optimizing frequencies between 20 and $3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ (close to the expected range of $1 5 \mathrm { - } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } ,$ generated $2 2 { \mathrm { ~ m W } } .$ Fig. 6(b) shows a linear rise with frequency up to $6 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ for the secondary impact type harvester's output power. The optimizing frequency of $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ generated $1 2 \mathrm { m W }$ of power, again in line with the expected results range $( 5 0 { - } 6 6 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ . The hitting type harvester's optimizing frequency of $4 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ generated $1 0 \mathrm { m W }$ and optimizing frequencies differed from the expected values. Fig. 6(c) shows the secondary impact type harvester delivering a linear power output rise up to $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ at $1 \ : \mathbf { M } \Omega$ . This optimizing frequency generated $1 . 3 \mathrm { m W }$ of power, which was once again within the expected range of $5 0 { \mathrm { - } } 6 6 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ At the hitting type harvester's optimizing frequency of $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , $0 . 7 8 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ of power was generated. As can be seen from the results shown here, the hitting type harvester's optimizing frequencies differed from the expected values. Although the secondary impact type harvester results showed that resistive load level had no effect on the optimizing frequency, optimizing power was affected by the resistive load. sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In the experiments described here, changes in the power output characteristics of a piezoelectric beam based on response to mechanical impulses and total displacement per unit time were investigated; the results showed that a secondary impact type harvester with higher total impulse per unit time and lower total displacement per unit time generated higher power outputs than a hitting type harvester at low resistive loads. On the other hand, a hitting type harvester with higher total displacement per unit time and lower total impulse per unit time generated higher power outputs than did a secondary impact type harvester at high resistive loads. However, under matched impedance conditions, the secondary impact type harvester generated higher power than the hitting type harvester. The results of the optimizing experiment show that the electrical power generated by the secondary impact type harvester increased linearly until the striking cycle equaled the duration of piezoelectric electricity generation. In the secondary impact type harvester, the fixed stick helped the cantilever beam to maintain a steady free vibrational frequency. Thus, the reproducibility of the secondary impact type harvester results was high. At $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and at the optimized frequency of the secondary impact type harvester at a low resistive load of $1 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , the generated output power was measured $1 2 4 \mathrm { m W } .$ ,which corresponds to power density of $1 4 0 \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ for entire cantilever beam and power density of $3 4 2 \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ for only piezoelectric material volume (including sliver paste volume).

In comparison to the linear response of the secondary impact type harvester, the hitting type harvester experienced interference; this occurred, in particular, when the striking frequency exceeded the generating frequency, which caused interference in the cantilever beam's vibrations from repeated hits. Because the vibration of the cantilever beam was irregular, reproducibility was decreased. At low resistive loads $( 1 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ , the optimizing frequency of the hitting type harvester was between 20 and $3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , and the output power of $2 2 \mathrm { m W }$ ,which corresponds to a $2 5 \mathrm { \ m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ power density for entire cantilever beam and power density of $6 0 \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ for only piezoelectric material volume (including sliver paste volume).

The experiments described in this paper demonstrated that in a piezoelectric harvester given a high total impulse per unit time with low total displacement per unit time, higher power outputs were generated at lower resistive loads. Conversely, for a harvester with high total displacement per unit time at a low total impulse per unit time, the power output was higher at high resistive loads. Power generation from secondary impact, instead of free vibration, is an effective means of reducing power output time in converting mechanical energy to electrical energy; this method is also effective in generating high levels of power.
